You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are a coding agent powered by the gpt-5.6-luna model.

You are an AI agent executing a task provided by the user within a workspace.

## Workspace layout

Everything you work with lives under one workspace root. **`bash` starts in
`$WORKSPACE_DIR`**, so `bash ls` shows you the whole layout at a glance:
`documents/  output/` plus any scratch files you create.

- **`$WORKSPACE_DIR`** — your working area, default `bash` cwd. Use it for
  notes and intermediate files.
- **`$DOCUMENTS_DIR`** (`$WORKSPACE_DIR/documents`) — task documents.
  Read-only.
- **`$OUTPUT_DIR`** (`$WORKSPACE_DIR/output`) — deliverables. Save every
  deliverable file here, including files you build with `bash` (.docx,
  .xlsx, .pptx): only files in `$OUTPUT_DIR` are delivered. `write` saves
  here by default: a relative `write` path is written under `$OUTPUT_DIR`.
- **Task configuration** (`task.json`) — contains the task definition and the
  grading rubric. Do not read, search, or reference it. Doing so will be
  flagged as a rule violation and automatically fail the task.

## Tool conventions

- `read` opens plain-text files only (.txt, .md, .eml, .csv, ...). To read
  .docx, .xlsx or .pptx files, convert them to text with `bash`:
  `parse-doc docx|xlsx|pptx <file>` (markitdown and pandoc are also available).
- Use `write` only for plain markdown — typically a `response.md`
  summarizing your work.
- Use `edit` for incremental refinement of a file you have already created.


Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one keeps the modification-time-ordered head.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

Use goal tools for one long-running completion objective in the current session. create_goal may infer goal intent from a direct human request in any language; do not create a goal for routine single-turn work. Call get_goal before update_goal and copy its exact goal_id and revision. After session resume or fork, an active goal is disarmed: when a human asks to continue or resume in any wording or language, use update_goal action resume to rearm it. Mark complete only when the objective is actually achieved. Mark blocked only after the same blocking condition persists for at least 3 consecutive goal rounds, and report that concrete condition in blocked_reason; difficulty, uncertainty, or useful remaining work is not blocked.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: create_goal
tools.description: Create one persisted same-session completion goal when the current direct human request is a long-running objective that should continue across autonomous goal rounds. You may infer that intent without requiring the user to say "create a goal". Do not use this for trivial single-turn work. Execution rejects non-human and subagent authority.

objective.description: The concrete completion objective inferred from the direct human request.

max_goal_rounds.description: Optional positive safe-integer limit on automatic continuation rounds.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: exit_plan_mode
tools.description: Use only in plan mode. Present your plan for the user's review and, on approval, leave plan mode. Send the COMPLETE plan as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it. The user may approve (carry out the plan from your next step) or keep planning — their feedback comes back in the tool result; revise and present again.

plan.description: The complete plan, as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it.

tools.name: get_goal
tools.description: Read the current same-session goal, including its exact id/revision, objective, phase, completed continuation rounds, round limit, blocker reason when present, and whether another continuation is armed. Call this before updating a goal.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result returns the first 100 paths in modification-time order, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: read_image
tools.description: Read a PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF file and return the image itself. A path without a file extension is accepted; the format is detected from the file content, so normalized attachment paths can be passed directly without copying or renaming. Harness validates and downscales large supported images before the next model request, so use this tool directly instead of installing image libraries or creating thumbnails merely to inspect an image. Independent files may be read concurrently in small batches. Requires the current model to accept image input.

file_path.description: Path to the image file, resolved by the filesystem backend.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: todo_write
tools.description: Record and update a structured task list for the current work. Send the ENTIRE list every call — it REPLACES the previous list (there are no partial updates, no per-item edits). Use it to plan multi-step work and show progress: add one todo per concrete step before you start. Mark every todo being actively worked on `in_progress` — several at once when work genuinely runs in parallel (e.g. concurrent subagents or background commands), one for sequential work; while work remains, at least one task should be `in_progress`. Mark a todo `completed` the moment it is done (do not batch completions), and allow no `in_progress` item only once all work is complete. Skip the list for trivial single-step tasks. Statuses: `pending` (not started), `in_progress` (being worked on now), `completed` (finished).

todos.description: The COMPLETE task list, replacing any previous list.

content.description: What the task is — a short imperative line.

tools.name: update_goal
tools.description: Update the exact current goal revision. edit, pause, and resume require a direct top-level human request. During an automatic continuation of the current goal, complete and blocked are also allowed. blocked is rejected before the configured minimum round count; the model remains responsible for judging that the same condition persisted across those rounds and must explain it in blocked_reason.

revision.description: Exact positive revision returned by get_goal.

objective.description: Replacement objective; valid only with action edit.

max_goal_rounds.description: Replacement cap; valid only with action edit.

blocked_reason.description: Concrete blocking condition; required only with action blocked.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file. A relative path is written under the output directory (`output/`): `response.md` is saved as `output/response.md`. An absolute path is used as is.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

73: **1.3.2 Orionis Analytics Ltd.**
74: 
75: **Orionis Analytics Ltd.** is an Irish limited company located at 14 Fitzwilliam Square East, Dublin 2, D02 W526, Ireland. 76: 
77: **Note for legal review regarding Orionis:** The DPA Template describes Orionis\'s services as \"anonymization and analytics.\" However, the DPA does not define or distinguish between \"anonymization\" and \"pseudonymization.\" This omission creates significant regulatory ambiguity. Under the GDPR, truly anonymized data falls outside the scope of the Regulation entirely (Recital 26), meaning that once data has been effectively and irreversibly anonymized, no GDPR obligations attach to its further processing, storage, or transfer. By contrast, pseudonymized data remains personal data subject to the full scope of GDPR obligations (Article 4(5), Recital 26).
78: 
79: The standard for effective anonymization established in Article 29 Working Party Opinion 05/2014 on Anonymisation Techniques (WP216, now endorsed by the European Data Protection Board) requires that data be rendered irreversibly incapable of identifying a data subject, considering all means reasonably likely to be used. The WP29 Opinion establishes a three-criteria test assessing the risks of (i) singling out, (ii) linkability, and (iii) inference. Data that does not satisfy all three criteria cannot be considered truly anonymized.
80: 
81: If Orionis\'s processing produces pseudonymized rather than truly anonymized outputs, those outputs remain personal data subject to the GDPR and must be covered by the DPA\'s processing terms. This includes all obligations related to international transfer mechanisms (if the data were subsequently transferred outside the EEA), security measures, data retention limitations, data subject rights facilitation, and breach notification. The DPA should define the anonymization standard by reference to objective and verifiable criteria, specify validation and certification requirements for Orionis\'s outputs, and expressly address the regulatory consequences if true anonymization is not achieved in practice.

Facebook Ireland Limited and Maximillian Schrenk* (Case C-311/18, \"Schrems II,\" July 16, 2020) and the EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 on measures that supplement transfer tools to ensure compliance with the EU level of protection of personal data (Version 2.0, adopted June 18, 2021), a TIA is required to assess whether the legal framework in the destination country (here, the United States) provides an essentially equivalent level of protection for personal data. Pinnacle should also consider requesting that Larkfield obtain DPF certification prior to the September 1, 2025 go-live date as an additional protective measure. *See Section 1.3.1, Diagram 3 (Section 3.3), and Summary Table (Section 4), Transfer #2.* \[References: \]
320: 
321: **4. International Transfer --- No Transfer Impact Assessment (High)**
322: 
323: The DPA Template does not require, reference, or document any Transfer Impact Assessment for transfers to the United States (Transfer #2) or for remote access from Singapore (Transfer #3). Following the CJEU\'s *Schrems II* judgment (Case C-311/18) and EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 (Version 2.0), a TIA is a prerequisite for reliance on SCCs as a transfer mechanism. The TIA must assess US and Singaporean surveillance laws, the availability of effective legal remedies, and the necessity of supplementary measures. The DPA must require the completion and documentation of a TIA for each identified international transfer, with provisions for periodic reassessment as the legal landscape evolves. *See Diagram 3 (Section 3.3), Diagram 4 (Section 3.4), and Summary Table (Section 4).* \[References: \]
324: 
325: **5. Anonymization Standard Undefined (Medium-High)**
326: 
327: Orionis Analytics Ltd. provides \"anonymization and analytics\" services, but the DPA Template does not define anonymization or distinguish it from pseudonymization. If Orionis\'s outputs are pseudonymized rather than truly anonymized under the standard established in WP29 Opinion 05/2014 (WP216, endorsed by the EDPB), those outputs remain personal data under the GDPR and are subject to all DPA obligations. The DPA must: (a) define the anonymization standard by reference to the WP29/EDPB three-criteria test (singling out, linkability, inference); (b) require Orionis to validate and certify that its outputs satisfy the defined standard; (c) specify that outputs failing to meet the standard are treated as personal data subject to all DPA protections; and (d) address whether pre-anonymization analytics processing requires separate lawful basis documentation. *See Section 1.3.2, Diagram 5 (Section 3.5), and Summary Table (Section 4), Transfer #4.* \[References: \]
328: 
329: **Scope Limitation:** This document focuses exclusively on data flow mapping and international transfer mechanism issues. Additional compliance gaps related to HIPAA Business Associate Agreement integration, breach notification timelines and thresholds, liability cap structure and allocation, CCPA/CPRA Service Provider provisions, audit rights and frequency, data deletion and return procedures, governing law and dispute resolution, DPO coordination requirements, and contractual survival periods are addressed in the separate compliance gap memorandum being prepared concurrently by this office and outside counsel.

**[Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc. --- Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH]{.underline}**
**[Data Processing Relationship]{.underline}**
**CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY-CLIENT PRIVILEGED / WORK PRODUCT**

This document is protected by the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine. Unauthorized disclosure, copying, or distribution is strictly prohibited. This document does not constitute legal advice to any third party.
**Prepared by:** Office of the General Counsel, Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc., 4200 Harborview Boulevard, Suite 1100, Austin, TX 78746
**Prepared for:** Internal use and for review by outside counsel Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP (Rachel Osterfeld, Partner), 900 K Street NW, Suite 700, Washington, DC 20001
**Date:** April 2025
**Reference Documents:**
> •Master Services Agreement dated March 15, 2024 (\"MSA\")
> •Stratosphere DPA Template Version 3.2 dated January 10, 2025 (received April 14, 2025) (\"DPA Template\" or \"DPA\")
> •Pinnacle US DPA Playbook (last updated February 28, 2025) (\"Playbook\")

**Purpose:** This document maps all personal data flows between Pinnacle (US and EU operations), Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH, and Stratosphere\'s subprocessors. The purpose of this mapping is to support the legal review of the DPA Template ahead of the May 16, 2025 internal review deadline and the September 1, 2025 EU expansion launch date. The data flow diagrams and accompanying analysis identify transfer mechanisms currently specified in the DPA Template, assess their legal sufficiency, and flag gaps requiring resolution prior to DPA execution.
Right-click to update Table of Contents
**[Section 1: Overview of Parties and Processing Relationship]{.underline}**

This section identifies each party involved in the processing of personal data under the proposed DPA, including the contractual and regulatory role of each party, the relevant legal frameworks, and key organizational details pertinent to the legal review.
**[1.1 Controllers]{.underline}**

**Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc.** is a Delaware corporation headquartered at 4200 Harborview Boulevard, Suite 1100, Austin, TX 78746. Pinnacle acts as a Controller under the General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) (\"GDPR\") for EU data subjects and as a HIPAA Covered Entity under 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164 for US Protected Health Information (\"PHI\"). Pinnacle has an annual revenue of approximately \$385 million and employs approximately 2,800 individuals.

**Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.** is a Netherlands-registered subsidiary located at Herengracht 450, 1017 CA Amsterdam, Netherlands. Pinnacle EU B.V. acts as a Controller under the GDPR with respect to EU data subjects. For purposes of the data flows described herein, EU personal data originates from Pinnacle EU B.V. and this entity serves as the data exporter in all EU-originating data flows.

For US data flows, Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc. acts as the HIPAA Covered Entity and, where applicable, as a Controller. For EU data flows, Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V. is the data exporter and Controller. The distinction between these two entities and their respective roles is critical for determining the appropriate transfer mechanisms, the applicable SCC module, and the regulatory obligations attaching to each data flow.
**[1.2 Processor]{.underline}**

**Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH** is a German limited liability company (Gesellschaft mit beschränkter Haftung) registered at Hohenzollernstraße 88, 80796 Munich, Germany (Handelsregister HRB 247891, Amtsgericht München). Stratosphere acts as Processor under the GDPR and as Business Associate under HIPAA. Stratosphere has an annual revenue of approximately €620 million and employs approximately 4,200 individuals across Germany, Ireland, and Singapore. The Chief Legal Officer is Dr. Florian Neumann. The appointed Data Protection Officer is Dr. Annika Vogt, reachable at dpo@stratospherecloud.example.com.
Stratosphere operates data center infrastructure at the following locations:
> •**Frankfurt, Germany** --- Primary data center for EU operations
> •**Dublin, Ireland** --- Redundant/failover data center for EU operations
> •**Northern Virginia, USA** --- Operated by subprocessor Larkfield Data Systems, LLC; used for US operations and EU disaster recovery

In addition, Stratosphere maintains a support engineering team based in **Singapore** that provides remote access technical support and incident resolution services. The Singapore-based personnel access data remotely; no data is stored at a Singapore facility.
Stratosphere holds the following relevant certifications:
> •**ISO 27001:2022** --- Certificate No. ISO-27001-SC-2024-0891, issued by TÜV Rheinland on June 15, 2024, valid through June 14, 2027.
> •**SOC 2 Type II** --- Report dated September 30, 2024, covering the audit period October 1, 2023 through September 30, 2024, issued by Clearwater Audit Partners GmbH.

These certifications cover Stratosphere\'s Frankfurt and Dublin data center operations. Counsel should confirm whether the certifications extend to the Northern Virginia facility operated by Larkfield and to the Singapore remote access operations.
**[1.3 Subprocessors]{.underline}**
The DPA Template identifies two subprocessors engaged by Stratosphere in connection with the services provided under the MSA. Each is described below with relevant observations for the legal review.
**1.3.1 Larkfield Data Systems, LLC**

**Larkfield Data Systems, LLC** is a Virginia limited liability company located at 7600 Prosperity Avenue, Fairfax, VA 22031. Larkfield provides database management and disaster recovery services to Stratosphere and operates the Northern Virginia data center used by Stratosphere for US data hosting and for EU disaster recovery replication.

**Important note (flagged for legal review):** Larkfield Data Systems, LLC is **NOT** certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (\"DPF\") (adequacy decision adopted by the European Commission on July 10, 2023, pursuant to Article 45(3) GDPR). This has direct implications for any EU personal data transferred to or accessible from the Northern Virginia data center. Because Larkfield is not a DPF participant, the DPF adequacy decision cannot serve as a transfer mechanism for data flows involving Larkfield as a data importer. Accordingly, Standard Contractual Clauses (with the correct module selection) remain the only viable transfer mechanism for EU data transfers to Larkfield, absent Larkfield obtaining DPF certification prior to the September 1, 2025 go-live date.
**1.3.2 Orionis Analytics Ltd.**

**Orionis Analytics Ltd.** is an Irish limited company located at 14 Fitzwilliam Square East, Dublin 2, D02 W526, Ireland. Orionis provides anonymization and analytics services to Stratosphere in connection with the processing of EU personal data. Orionis operates exclusively from its Dublin location within the EEA.

**Note for legal review regarding Orionis:** The DPA Template describes Orionis\'s services as \"anonymization and analytics.\" However, the DPA does not define or distinguish between \"anonymization\" and \"pseudonymization.\" This omission creates significant regulatory ambiguity. Under the GDPR, truly anonymized data falls outside the scope of the Regulation entirely (Recital 26), meaning that once data has been effectively and irreversibly anonymized, no GDPR obligations attach to its further processing, storage, or transfer. By contrast, pseudonymized data remains personal data subject to the full scope of GDPR obligations (Article 4(5), Recital 26).

The standard for effective anonymization established in Article 29 Working Party Opinion 05/2014 on Anonymisation Techniques (WP216, now endorsed by the European Data Protection Board) requires that data be rendered irreversibly incapable of identifying a data subject, considering all means reasonably likely to be used. The WP29 Opinion establishes a three-criteria test assessing the risks of (i) singling out, (ii) linkability, and (iii) inference. Data that does not satisfy all three criteria cannot be considered truly anonymized.

If Orionis\'s processing produces pseudonymized rather than truly anonymized outputs, those outputs remain personal data subject to the GDPR and must be covered by the DPA\'s processing terms. This includes all obligations related to international transfer mechanisms (if the data were subsequently transferred outside the EEA), security measures, data retention limitations, data subject rights facilitation, and breach notification. The DPA should define the anonymization standard by reference to objective and verifiable criteria, specify validation and certification requirements for Orionis\'s outputs, and expressly address the regulatory consequences if true anonymization is not achieved in practice.
**[Section 2: Data Categories and Data Subject Populations]{.underline}**

This section identifies the categories of personal data processed and the populations of data subjects whose data is involved in the processing relationship. This information is necessary for the legal review of the DPA Template to assess whether the DPA accurately and completely describes the scope of processing.
**[2.1 EU Data Subjects and Data Categories]{.underline}**
**2.1.1 EU Patient Data**
> •**Projected data subject volume (Year 1):** Approximately 150,000 data subjects
> •**Data categories:** Names, dates of birth, health insurance identifiers, medical record numbers, diagnosis codes (ICD-10), treatment histories

> •**Special category data under GDPR Article 9:** Yes --- the data includes health data, specifically diagnosis codes and treatment histories, which constitute special categories of personal data within the meaning of Article 9(1) GDPR. Processing of such data requires an Article 9(2) exemption, and a Data Protection Impact Assessment is likely required under Article 35(3)(b) GDPR (processing of special category data on a large scale).
> •**Data origin:** Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V. (Amsterdam, Netherlands)
> •**Storage locations:** Stratosphere Frankfurt data center (Germany); Stratosphere Dublin data center (Ireland)
**2.1.2 EU Healthcare Provider Contact Data**
> •**Data subject volume:** Approximately 320 data subjects

> •**Data categories:** Names, professional email addresses, professional telephone numbers, professional mailing addresses, professional identifiers (e.g., registration numbers with national medical boards)
> •**Special category data under GDPR Article 9:** No
> •**Data origin:** Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V. (Amsterdam, Netherlands)
> •**Storage locations:** Stratosphere Frankfurt data center (Germany); Stratosphere Dublin data center (Ireland)
**[2.2 US Data Subjects and Data Categories]{.underline}**
**2.2.1 US Patient Data / Protected Health Information (PHI)**
> •**Data subject volume:** Approximately 2.1 million data subjects

> •**Data categories:** Names, dates of birth, health insurance identifiers, medical record numbers, diagnosis codes (ICD-10), treatment histories, and other data elements constituting Protected Health Information under the definition set forth in 45 CFR § 160.103
> •**HIPAA classification:** Protected Health Information (PHI). All 18 HIPAA identifiers may be present.
> •**Data origin:** Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc. (Austin, TX)
> •**Storage location:** Northern Virginia data center, operated by Larkfield Data Systems, LLC (Fairfax, VA)
**2.2.2 US Healthcare Provider Contact Data**
> •**Data subject volume:** Approximately 14,000 data subjects
> •**Data categories:** Names, professional contact information (email addresses, telephone numbers, mailing addresses), professional identifiers (NPI numbers, state license numbers)
> •**Data origin:** Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc. (Austin, TX)
> •**Storage location:** Northern Virginia data center, operated by Larkfield Data Systems, LLC (Fairfax, VA)
**2.2.3 California Residents Subset**

Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately 890,000 California residents, which constitutes a subset of the US patient data and US healthcare provider contact data populations described above. This subset is subject to the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020 (collectively, \"CCPA/CPRA\"). Under the CCPA/CPRA, Stratosphere and Larkfield function as \"Service Providers\" and are subject to the corresponding obligations, including restrictions on selling or sharing personal information, use limitations, and cooperation with consumer rights requests.
**[Section 3: Data Flow Diagrams]{.underline}**

This section provides detailed textual descriptions of each data flow between and among the parties identified in Section 1. Each data flow diagram is described in sufficient detail for a reviewing attorney to understand the origin, destination, content, purpose, encryption standards, and applicable transfer mechanisms without reference to a visual graphic. Where gaps or issues have been identified, they are flagged for the legal review team.
**[3.1 Diagram 1 --- EU Data Flow (Primary Processing)]{.underline}**
**Flow Description:**

The primary EU data flow originates at **Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.** (Amsterdam, Netherlands), acting in its capacity as Controller. EU patient data and EU healthcare provider contact data are transmitted via encrypted connection using Transport Layer Security (TLS) version 1.3 to two destinations within the European Economic Area:

**Destination 1:** The data is transmitted to the **Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH Frankfurt Data Center** located in Frankfurt, Germany. This facility serves as the primary storage location for all EU personal data. Data is encrypted at rest using AES-256 encryption. Stratosphere acts as Processor at this location.

**Destination 2:** The data is simultaneously or subsequently replicated to the **Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH Dublin Data Center** located in Dublin, Ireland. This facility serves as the redundant storage and failover location for EU personal data. Data is encrypted at rest using AES-256 encryption. Stratosphere acts as Processor at this location.

**Intra-EEA Transfer:** The data replication between the Frankfurt data center and the Dublin data center constitutes an intra-EEA transfer. Both Germany and Ireland are Member States of the European Union and part of the European Economic Area. No international transfer mechanism under GDPR Chapter V is required for this data flow.
**Processing Activities:** Cloud hosting, managed database services, structured and unstructured data storage, scheduled and on-demand backup, system monitoring, and performance optimization.
**Transfer Mechanism Required:** None --- this is an intra-EEA processing arrangement.
**[3.2 Diagram 2 --- US Data Flow (Primary Processing)]{.underline}**
**Flow Description:**

The primary US data flow originates at **Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc.** (Austin, TX), acting in its capacity as HIPAA Covered Entity and Controller. US patient PHI and US healthcare provider contact data are transmitted via encrypted connection using TLS 1.3 to a single destination within the United States:

**Destination:** The data is transmitted to the **Northern Virginia Data Center** located in Fairfax, Virginia, which is owned and operated by **Larkfield Data Systems, LLC**. Larkfield acts as a Subprocessor under the GDPR framework and as a Business Associate sub-contractor under HIPAA. Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH accesses and manages the data hosted at the Larkfield Northern Virginia facility pursuant to the terms of the MSA.

**Processing Activities:** Database management, disaster recovery services, structured and unstructured data storage, scheduled and on-demand backup, data replication for business continuity purposes, and system monitoring.

**Cross-Border Transfer:** All US data remains within the United States throughout this data flow. No cross-border or international transfer occurs in connection with primary US processing. Accordingly, no GDPR Chapter V transfer mechanism is required.

**Regulatory Note:** Although no GDPR international transfer mechanism is required for this flow, the HIPAA Business Associate Agreement (\"BAA\") obligations must flow down from Stratosphere to Larkfield. The adequacy of this BAA flow-down is addressed in the separate compliance gap memorandum and is not within the scope of this data flow document.
**[3.3 Diagram 3 --- Cross-Border Transfer: Frankfurt to Northern Virginia (Disaster Recovery)]{.underline}**
**Flow Description:**

This data flow involves the transfer of EU-originating data from within the EEA to a facility located in the United States. It constitutes an international transfer of personal data under GDPR Chapter V and requires a valid transfer mechanism.

**Source:** The data originates from the **Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH Frankfurt Data Center** (Frankfurt, Germany), where Stratosphere acts as Processor within the EEA. The datasets transferred consist of aggregated and pseudonymized datasets derived from EU personal data originally provided by Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.

**Transmission:** The data is transmitted via encrypted connection to the destination facility. The DPA Template does not specify the encryption protocol for this particular transfer; counsel should confirm that TLS 1.3 or equivalent encryption is applied.

**Destination:** The data is received at the **Northern Virginia Data Center** (Fairfax, VA), operated by **Larkfield Data Systems, LLC**. Larkfield acts as Subprocessor. The data center is located outside the European Economic Area.

**Purpose:** Disaster recovery and business continuity. The transferred datasets are maintained at the Northern Virginia facility to ensure service continuity in the event of a catastrophic failure at the Frankfurt or Dublin data centers.

**Transfer Mechanism in DPA Template:** The DPA Template (Section 7) references the EU Standard Contractual Clauses adopted pursuant to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of June 4, 2021. However, the DPA Template attaches only **Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor)** of the 2021 SCCs.

**FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- Transfer Mechanism Gap :** This transfer is from **Stratosphere (Processor)** to **Larkfield (Subprocessor)**. The DPA Template attaches only SCC Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor), which governs transfers from a Controller to a Processor. However, this specific transfer is a Processor-to-Subprocessor transfer, which requires **SCC Module 3 (Processor-to-Subprocessor)** under Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914. The 2021 SCCs contain four modules designed for distinct transfer scenarios: Module 1 (Controller-to-Controller), Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor), Module 3 (Processor-to-Subprocessor), and Module 4 (Processor-to-Controller). Module 2 alone is legally insufficient for this transfer scenario. Module 3 must be separately executed between Stratosphere (as data exporter/Processor) and Larkfield (as data importer/Subprocessor), with Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V. as the ultimate Controller having enforceable rights under the SCCs as a third-party beneficiary. The failure to include Module 3 means there is currently no valid transfer mechanism in place for this data flow.

**FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- Larkfield DPF Status :** Larkfield Data Systems, LLC is **NOT** certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. The European Commission\'s adequacy decision for the DPF (adopted July 10, 2023) can only be relied upon where the data importer is a certified participant in the DPF program. Because Larkfield has not obtained DPF certification, the DPF adequacy decision cannot serve as an alternative transfer mechanism for this transfer. SCCs (with the correct Module 3 selection) remain the only viable mechanism for this transfer, unless Larkfield obtains DPF certification prior to the September 1, 2025 go-live date.

**FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- No Transfer Impact Assessment :** The DPA Template does not require, reference, or document any Transfer Impact Assessment (\"TIA\") for this transfer. Following the Court of Justice of the European Union\'s judgment in *Data Protection Commissioner v. Facebook Ireland Limited and Maximillian Schrenk* (Case C-311/18, \"Schrems II,\" July 16, 2020) and the EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 on measures that supplement transfer tools to ensure compliance with the EU level of protection of personal data (Version 2.0, adopted June 18, 2021), a TIA is required to assess whether the legal framework in the destination country (here, the United States) provides an essentially equivalent level of protection for personal data. The TIA must specifically assess US surveillance laws (including Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act and Executive Order 12333), the availability of redress mechanisms (including those established by Executive Order 14086 and the Data Protection Review Court), and any supplementary technical, organizational, or contractual measures needed to address identified risks. No TIA has been prepared, referenced, or required by the DPA Template for any international transfer.

**Additional Note Regarding Pseudonymized Data:** Although the datasets transferred to the Northern Virginia facility are described in the DPA Template as \"aggregated and pseudonymized,\" it is essential to recognize that pseudonymized data remains personal data under the GDPR (Article 4(5), Recital 26) and requires a valid transfer mechanism under Chapter V. Only data that has been truly and irreversibly anonymized in accordance with the standard articulated in WP29 Opinion 05/2014 (WP216) would fall outside the scope of the GDPR and thereby not require a transfer mechanism. The characterization of data as \"pseudonymized\" does not reduce or eliminate the requirement for SCCs or another valid transfer mechanism. See also the flag regarding Orionis and the anonymization/pseudonymization distinction in Section 1.3 above.
**[3.4 Diagram 4 --- Cross-Border Access: Singapore Remote Access to EU Data]{.underline}**
**Flow Description:**

This data flow involves remote access by Stratosphere personnel located outside the EEA to EU personal data stored within the EEA. Although no data is physically transferred to or stored in Singapore, remote access from a third country constitutes a \"transfer\" of personal data under the GDPR, as confirmed by EDPB guidance.

**Accessor:** **Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH support engineers based in Singapore.** These individuals are employees or contractors of Stratosphere acting in their capacity as Processor personnel. Singapore is not an EU Member State and is not part of the European Economic Area.

**Access Method:** Remote access via encrypted VPN tunnel using TLS 1.3 to the Frankfurt and/or Dublin data centers. The Singapore-based engineers access EU personal data for the purposes of incident resolution and technical support. Data is viewed and, in some cases, modified remotely but is not copied to or stored at any Singapore facility.

**Data Location:** The EU personal data remains physically stored at the **Stratosphere Frankfurt Data Center** (Germany) and/or the **Stratosphere Dublin Data Center** (Ireland), both within the EEA.
**Purpose:** Incident resolution, technical troubleshooting, and technical support services.

**Nature of Access as International Transfer:** Although the data is not physically relocated to Singapore, remote access from a third country to personal data stored within the EEA constitutes an international transfer under the GDPR within the meaning of Chapter V. The EDPB has consistently treated such remote access scenarios as transfers requiring a valid legal mechanism. Singapore is not covered by an EU adequacy decision under Article 45 GDPR.

**FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- Singapore Access Not Addressed :** The DPA Template does not address the Singapore remote access scenario at all. DPA Section 7, which governs international transfers, is entirely silent on the existence of Stratosphere personnel in Singapore and on any remote access from Singapore to EU personal data stored in Frankfurt or Dublin. This constitutes a compliance gap.
Because Singapore is not the subject of an EU adequacy decision, a valid transfer mechanism under GDPR Chapter V must be established for this data flow. The available options include:

> \(i\) Executing SCCs under Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914, likely Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor), with Stratosphere\'s Singapore operations designated as an additional data importer. Module 2 would be appropriate because the Singapore-based personnel are Processor employees accessing data on behalf of the Controller. Supplementary measures specific to the Singapore legal environment should be incorporated.

> \(ii\) Relying on derogations under GDPR Article 49. However, Article 49 derogations are interpreted narrowly and are generally not available for systematic or repetitive transfers. Because Singapore-based support engineers access EU data on a regular and ongoing basis for incident resolution, Article 49 derogations are unlikely to provide a sustainable legal basis.

> \(iii\) Implementing supplementary technical measures that limit the scope and nature of data accessible from Singapore, such as restricting Singapore-based personnel to anonymized or non-personal diagnostic data only, or restricting access to metadata without access to identifiable patient records.

> \(iv\) Alternatively, Stratosphere could restrict all access to EU personal data to personnel located within the EEA, thereby eliminating the need for a transfer mechanism for this scenario. This would require contractual commitment in the DPA and operational verification.
The current DPA Template\'s silence on this transfer constitutes a material compliance gap that must be resolved prior to DPA execution and the September 1, 2025 EU expansion launch date.
**[3.5 Diagram 5 --- EU Data to Orionis Analytics (Anonymization and Analytics)]{.underline}**
**Flow Description:**
This data flow involves the transfer of EU personal data from Stratosphere to Orionis Analytics Ltd. for anonymization and analytics processing. Both parties operate within the EEA.
**Source:** **Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH** --- Frankfurt Data Center (Germany) and/or Dublin Data Center (Ireland), acting as Processor.

**Transmission:** EU personal data is transferred to Orionis for anonymization and analytics processing. The DPA Template does not specify the encryption protocol or method for this specific intra-EEA transfer; counsel should confirm that appropriate technical measures are in place.
**Destination:** **Orionis Analytics Ltd.** --- Dublin, Ireland, acting as Subprocessor.
**Purpose:** Anonymization and analytics services as described in the DPA Template.

**Nature of Transfer:** This is an intra-EEA transfer from Germany/Ireland to Ireland. Both the data exporter (Stratosphere, Frankfurt/Dublin) and the data importer (Orionis, Dublin) are located within the European Economic Area. No GDPR Chapter V international transfer mechanism is required.

**FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- Anonymization vs. Pseudonymization :** Data sent to Orionis for \"anonymization\" is personal data at the point of transfer and must be protected accordingly under the GDPR. The critical question is whether Orionis\'s output constitutes truly anonymized data (which would fall outside the scope of the GDPR) or pseudonymized data (which remains personal data subject to the full panoply of GDPR obligations).
The DPA must be amended to address this issue comprehensively. Specifically, the DPA should:

> \(1\) Define the anonymization standard by reference to objective and verifiable criteria, including the three-criteria test established in WP29 Opinion 05/2014 (WP216): (a) singling out --- it should not be possible to isolate an individual from the dataset; (b) linkability --- it should not be possible to link records relating to the same individual across datasets; and (c) inference --- it should not be possible to deduce information about an individual from the data with significant probability.
> \(2\) Require Orionis to validate and certify that its outputs meet the defined anonymization standard, with such validation to be documented and made available to Pinnacle EU B.V. upon request.

> \(3\) Specify that if Orionis\'s outputs do not meet the defined anonymization standard, those outputs shall be treated as \"Personal Data\" under the DPA and shall remain subject to all DPA obligations, including security measures, data retention limits, data subject rights facilitation, breach notification, and, if transferred outside the EEA at any future point, international transfer mechanisms.

> \(4\) Address whether the analytics processing performed on data prior to the completion of the anonymization process constitutes a separate processing activity requiring its own documentation of lawful basis and purpose limitation under Articles 5(1)(b) and 6 GDPR.
**[Section 4: Summary of International Transfers Requiring Legal Mechanisms]{.underline}**

The following table consolidates all data flows identified in Section 3, with particular focus on cross-border transfers requiring a legal mechanism under GDPR Chapter V. For each transfer, the table identifies the exporter, importer, their respective roles, the destination country, the transfer mechanism currently referenced in the DPA Template, the required mechanism, and whether a gap has been identified.

Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH                 Controller                    Processor                          Germany / Ireland (EEA)   N/A (intra-EEA)         None required                                                No

**Key Observations:**

**Larkfield DPF Certification Status.** Larkfield Data Systems, LLC is **NOT** certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (adequacy decision adopted by the European Commission on July 10, 2023). Accordingly, the DPF adequacy decision cannot serve as an alternative or supplementary transfer mechanism for Transfer #2. The only viable mechanism for Transfer #2 is the execution of properly completed SCCs under Module 3 (Processor-to-Subprocessor), accompanied by a Transfer Impact Assessment and appropriate supplementary measures.

**Absence of Transfer Impact Assessment.** No Transfer Impact Assessment is referenced, required, or documented anywhere in the DPA Template for any of the identified international transfers. This applies to both Transfer #2 (Frankfurt to Northern Virginia) and Transfer #3 (Singapore remote access to Frankfurt/Dublin). Post-Schrems II, a TIA is a prerequisite for reliance on SCCs as a transfer mechanism.

**Incorrect SCC Module Selection.** The DPA Template references Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 and attaches only Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor) SCCs. While Module 2 may be appropriate for the direct Controller-to-Processor relationship between Pinnacle EU B.V. and Stratosphere (although that relationship does not involve an international transfer), it is not appropriate for the Processor-to-Subprocessor transfer between Stratosphere and Larkfield. Module 3 (Processor-to-Subprocessor) must be separately executed for Transfer #2, with Pinnacle EU B.V. designated as the Controller with enforceable third-party beneficiary rights.
**[Section 5: Data Volume and Regulatory Applicability Summary]{.underline}**

The following table summarizes the data subject populations, approximate data volumes, applicable regulatory frameworks, primary storage locations, and key regulatory notes for each data category involved in the processing relationship.
**Data Population**                   **Approx. Volume**              **Applicable Regulations**                                        **Storage Location(s)**         **Key Regulatory Notes**

EU Patients                           \~150,000 (Year 1 projection)   GDPR (including Art. 9 --- special categories of personal data)   Frankfurt (DE), Dublin (IE)     Health data constitutes special category data; DPIA likely required under Art. 35(3)(b); explicit consent or Art. 9(2)(h) exemption required

EU Healthcare Providers               \~320                           GDPR                                                              Frankfurt (DE), Dublin (IE)     Standard personal data; legitimate interest or contractual necessity likely sufficient

US Patients (PHI)                     \~2.1 million                   HIPAA (45 CFR Parts 160, 164); applicable state privacy laws      Northern Virginia (Larkfield)   PHI --- BAA required; Stratosphere is Business Associate; Larkfield is BA sub-contractor

US Healthcare Providers               \~14,000                        Applicable state privacy laws; contractual obligations            Northern Virginia (Larkfield)   Professional contact data; standard contractual protections apply

California Residents (subset of US)   \~890,000                       CCPA/CPRA (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100 et seq.)                     Northern Virginia (Larkfield)   Service Provider obligations under CCPA/CPRA apply to Stratosphere and Larkfield; restrictions on sale/sharing of PI

**Financial Context:** The MSA annual fees total \$4.2 million, allocated as \$2.8 million for US services and \$1.4 million for EU services. This financial context is relevant to the proportionality assessment for liability cap negotiations addressed in the separate compliance gap memorandum.

**Timeline Note:** The EU expansion launch date is **September 1, 2025**. The DPA must be fully negotiated, executed, and compliant with all applicable GDPR requirements --- including valid international transfer mechanisms for all identified cross-border data flows --- before this date. The internal review deadline for the DPA Template is **May 16, 2025**, which allows approximately four months for negotiation and finalization prior to the launch date.
**[Section 6: Observations and Flags for Legal Review]{.underline}**

This section provides a consolidated list of all issues identified through the data flow mapping exercise described in this document. Each issue is cross-referenced to the relevant DPA Template section, the data flow diagram(s) in which the issue was identified, and the internal issue tracking reference. These flags are intended for use by the legal team in preparing the compliance gap memorandum and DPA redline.
**1. International Transfer --- Wrong SCC Module (Critical)**

The Processor-to-Subprocessor transfer from Stratosphere (Frankfurt data center) to Larkfield (Northern Virginia data center) for disaster recovery and business continuity purposes requires **SCC Module 3 (Processor-to-Subprocessor)** under Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914. The DPA Template (Section 7) references and attaches only Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor), which is legally insufficient for this transfer scenario. Module 3 must be separately executed between Stratosphere (as Processor/data exporter) and Larkfield (as Subprocessor/data importer), with Pinnacle EU B.V. designated as the Controller with enforceable third-party beneficiary rights under the SCCs. Without the correct Module 3 SCCs in place, there is no valid legal mechanism for this transfer under GDPR Chapter V. *See Diagram 3 (Section 3.3) and Summary Table (Section 4), Transfer #2.*.
**2. International Transfer --- Singapore Remote Access Not Covered (High)**

Stratosphere support engineers based in Singapore access EU personal data stored at the Frankfurt and Dublin data centers on a regular basis for incident resolution and technical support. This remote access constitutes an international transfer under the GDPR. No transfer mechanism is specified, referenced, or contemplated in the DPA Template for this scenario. DPA Section 7 is entirely silent on Singapore. The DPA must include a valid GDPR Chapter V mechanism (most likely Module 2 SCCs with Singapore-specific supplementary measures) or Stratosphere must contractually commit to restricting EU data access to EEA-based personnel exclusively. *See Diagram 4 (Section 3.4) and Summary Table (Section 4), Transfer #3.* \[References: \]
**3. International Transfer --- Larkfield Not DPF-Certified (High)**

Larkfield Data Systems, LLC is not certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. The DPF adequacy decision (adopted July 10, 2023) cannot be relied upon as an alternative or supplementary transfer mechanism for any data flows involving Larkfield as the data importer. SCCs under Module 3, accompanied by supplementary measures and a Transfer Impact Assessment, are required. Pinnacle should also consider requesting that Larkfield obtain DPF certification prior to the September 1, 2025 go-live date as an additional protective measure. *See Section 1.3.1, Diagram 3 (Section 3.3), and Summary Table (Section 4), Transfer #2.* \[References: \]
**4. International Transfer --- No Transfer Impact Assessment (High)**

The DPA Template does not require, reference, or document any Transfer Impact Assessment for transfers to the United States (Transfer #2) or for remote access from Singapore (Transfer #3). Following the CJEU\'s *Schrems II* judgment (Case C-311/18) and EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 (Version 2.0), a TIA is a prerequisite for reliance on SCCs as a transfer mechanism. The TIA must assess US and Singaporean surveillance laws, the availability of effective legal remedies, and the necessity of supplementary measures. The DPA must require the completion and documentation of a TIA for each identified international transfer, with provisions for periodic reassessment as the legal landscape evolves. *See Diagram 3 (Section 3.3), Diagram 4 (Section 3.4), and Summary Table (Section 4).* \[References: \]
**5. Anonymization Standard Undefined (Medium-High)**

Orionis Analytics Ltd. provides \"anonymization and analytics\" services, but the DPA Template does not define anonymization or distinguish it from pseudonymization. If Orionis\'s outputs are pseudonymized rather than truly anonymized under the standard established in WP29 Opinion 05/2014 (WP216, endorsed by the EDPB), those outputs remain personal data under the GDPR and are subject to all DPA obligations. The DPA must: (a) define the anonymization standard by reference to the WP29/EDPB three-criteria test (singling out, linkability, inference); (b) require Orionis to validate and certify that its outputs satisfy the defined standard; (c) specify that outputs failing to meet the standard are treated as personal data subject to all DPA protections; and (d) address whether pre-anonymization analytics processing requires separate lawful basis documentation. *See Section 1.3.2, Diagram 5 (Section 3.5), and Summary Table (Section 4), Transfer #4.* \[References: \]

**Scope Limitation:** This document focuses exclusively on data flow mapping and international transfer mechanism issues. Additional compliance gaps related to HIPAA Business Associate Agreement integration, breach notification timelines and thresholds, liability cap structure and allocation, CCPA/CPRA Service Provider provisions, audit rights and frequency, data deletion and return procedures, governing law and dispute resolution, DPO coordination requirements, and contractual survival periods are addressed in the separate compliance gap memorandum being prepared concurrently by this office and outside counsel.

36:

Orionis Analytics Ltd. provides data anonymization pipelines and analytics support to Stratosphere in connection with the EU Services.

In connection with Stratosphere\'s business continuity program, certain aggregated and pseudonymized datasets are transferred from the Frankfurt, Germany data center to the Northern Virginia Facility for disaster recovery and business continuity purposes. The specific datasets and transfer mechanisms are documented in Exhibit B (Technical Specifications) to the MSA.

45: **Support Services:** Stratosphere provides managed support services on a 24/7 basis, including through support engineers based in Singapore who may remotely access system data for purposes of incident detection, diagnosis, and resolution. 69: **MSA General Liability Cap:** Each party\'s total aggregate liability for all claims of any kind arising under or in connection with the MSA (excluding claims arising under the Data Processing Agreement) shall not exceed the greater of: (a) Five Million US Dollars (\$5,000,000); or (b) the total fees actually paid and payable by Client to Service Provider in the twelve (12)-month period immediately preceding the event giving rise to the claim.

71: **Exclusions from MSA General Liability Cap:** The foregoing MSA general liability cap shall not apply to: (i) a party\'s indemnification obligations with respect to third-party intellectual property infringement claims under Section 14 of the MSA; (ii) liability arising from a party\'s breach of the confidentiality obligations set forth in Section 6 of the MSA (which liability is subject to a separate super-cap equal to two times (2x) the total annual fees payable under the MSA); (iii) liability arising from a party\'s fraud, gross negligence, or willful misconduct; and (iv) a party\'s obligations to pay fees and expenses properly due and owing under the MSA.

73: **DPA Liability --- Separate Treatment:** The MSA expressly provides that liability arising from data protection obligations shall be governed exclusively by the terms of the Data Processing Agreement, to be executed as Exhibit D to the MSA (see Section 9 below). The MSA general liability cap does not apply to, and does not subsume, any DPA-specific liability provisions. *Note: The DPA template provided by Stratosphere (Version 3.2, dated January 10, 2025) proposes a separate aggregate data protection liability cap of €500,000 (approximately \$545,000 at current exchange rates). This DPA-specific cap is substantially below the MSA general liability cap and is subject to ongoing negotiation between the parties.*

75: **Consequential Damages Exclusion:** The MSA contains a mutual exclusion of liability for indirect, incidental, consequential, special, exemplary, and punitive damages, including without limitation lost profits, lost revenue, and loss of business opportunity. This mutual exclusion is subject to carve-outs for: (i) breaches of confidentiality obligations under Section 6 of the MSA; (ii) third-party intellectual property indemnification obligations under Section 14 of the MSA; and (iii) liability arising from fraud, gross negligence, or willful misconduct.

The confidentiality obligations survive for a period of three (3) years following the expiration or termination of the MSA. Standard carve-outs apply for information that is or becomes publicly available without breach by the receiving party, is independently developed by the receiving party without reference to Confidential Information, is lawfully obtained from a third party without restriction, or is required to be disclosed by applicable law, regulation, or valid legal process. The confidentiality provisions of the MSA do not limit, replace, or otherwise affect either party\'s data protection obligations under the Data Processing Agreement.

The seat (legal place) of arbitration shall be New York, New York. The arbitral tribunal shall consist of three (3) arbitrators appointed in accordance with the AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules. The language of the arbitration shall be English. The award rendered by the arbitral tribunal shall be final and binding on the parties, and judgment upon the award may be entered in any court of competent jurisdiction.

This complexity is noted for purposes of the ongoing DPA negotiation.*

114: 
115: **Stratosphere\'s Outside Counsel for DPA Negotiation:** Voss Kellner Rechtsanwälte, Maximilianstraße 35, 80539 Munich, Germany (lead partner: Dr. Karin Beckert).

117: **Stratosphere Data Protection Officer:** Dr. Annika Vogt, Data Protection Officer, Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH (contact: dpo@stratospherecloud.example.com).

The certification covers Stratosphere\'s cloud hosting and managed database services operations at its Frankfurt, Germany and Dublin, Ireland data centers.

Report dated September 30, 2024, covering the audit period from October 1, 2023 through September 30, 2024, issued by Clearwater Audit Partners GmbH (Munich). Any material changes to the scope of Stratosphere\'s certifications or any failure to maintain or renew such certifications shall be promptly communicated to Pinnacle in writing.

131: **Termination for Material Breach:** Either party may terminate the MSA upon written notice to the other party if the other party commits a material breach of the MSA and fails to cure such breach within thirty (30) days after receipt of written notice specifying the nature of the breach in reasonable detail.

The parties agree that electronic signatures shall have the same legal force and effect as original ink signatures.
