**EU Expansion Note:** Pinnacle\'s EU Services under the MSA are expected to commence on or about September 1, 2025 (the \"EU Go-Live Date\"), subject to the completion of all regulatory and contractual prerequisites, including without limitation the execution of a fully conforming Data Processing Agreement between the parties (see Section 9 below for current status and additional detail regarding the DPA).
**[Section 3 --- Service Descriptions]{.underline}**

**US Services:** Cloud hosting and managed database services for Pinnacle\'s US-based digital health platform, supporting the processing of data relating to approximately 2.1 million US patients and approximately 14,000 US healthcare provider contacts. All US data is hosted and stored at the Northern Virginia data center operated by Stratosphere\'s authorized subcontractor, Larkfield Data Systems, LLC, located at 7600 Prosperity Avenue, Fairfax, VA 22031 (the \"Northern Virginia Facility\").

**EU Services:** Cloud hosting, managed database services, and analytics support for Pinnacle\'s EU operations (contracted through Pinnacle EU B.V.), supporting the processing of data relating to a projected approximately 150,000 EU-based patients and approximately 320 EU-based healthcare provider contacts in Year 1 of EU operations. EU data is hosted and stored at Stratosphere\'s own data centers located in Frankfurt, Germany and Dublin, Ireland, respectively.

**Analytics Support:** Anonymization and analytics services are provided through Stratosphere\'s authorized subcontractor, Orionis Analytics Ltd., a company incorporated in Ireland with its registered office at 14 Fitzwilliam Square East, Dublin 2, D02 W526, Ireland. Orionis Analytics Ltd. provides data anonymization pipelines and analytics support to Stratosphere in connection with the EU Services.

**Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity:** Database management and disaster recovery services are provided through Larkfield Data Systems, LLC at the Northern Virginia Facility. In connection with Stratosphere\'s business continuity program, certain aggregated and pseudonymized datasets are transferred from the Frankfurt, Germany data center to the Northern Virginia Facility for disaster recovery and business continuity purposes. The specific datasets and transfer mechanisms are documented in Exhibit B (Technical Specifications) to the MSA.

**Support Services:** Stratosphere provides managed support services on a 24/7 basis, including through support engineers based in Singapore who may remotely access system data for purposes of incident detection, diagnosis, and resolution. Remote access by Singapore-based personnel is subject to Stratosphere\'s internal access control policies as documented in the MSA\'s Exhibit C (Security Requirements).
**[Section 4 --- Fee Structure]{.underline}**
**Total Annual Service Fees:** The total annual service fees payable by Pinnacle under the MSA are Four Million Two Hundred Thousand US Dollars (\$4,200,000), allocated as follows:
**Service Category**                **Annual Fee (USD)**
US Services                         \$2,800,000
EU Services                         \$1,400,000
**Total Annual Fees**               **\$4,200,000**

**Payment Terms:** Service fees are invoiced quarterly in advance by Stratosphere. All invoices are due and payable within thirty (30) days from the date of invoice (Net 30). Late payments are subject to interest at the rate of 1.5% per month or the maximum rate permitted by applicable law, whichever is lower.

**Fee Adjustments:** Annual fee adjustments, if any, are subject to mutual written agreement between the parties during the applicable renewal notice period. There is no automatic Consumer Price Index (CPI) escalator during the Initial Term. Fee adjustments for any Renewal Term shall be proposed by the requesting party in writing no later than one hundred twenty (120) days prior to the commencement of such Renewal Term.

**EU Services Fee Commencement:** EU Services fees shall commence upon the EU Go-Live Date (targeted for September 1, 2025). Pro-rata adjustments shall apply for any partial quarter in which EU Services commence, calculated on a daily basis within the applicable quarterly period.
**[Section 5 --- General Liability Cap (MSA-Level)]{.underline}**

**MSA General Liability Cap:** Each party\'s total aggregate liability for all claims of any kind arising under or in connection with the MSA (excluding claims arising under the Data Processing Agreement) shall not exceed the greater of: (a) Five Million US Dollars (\$5,000,000); or (b) the total fees actually paid and payable by Client to Service Provider in the twelve (12)-month period immediately preceding the event giving rise to the claim.

**Exclusions from MSA General Liability Cap:** The foregoing MSA general liability cap shall not apply to: (i) a party\'s indemnification obligations with respect to third-party intellectual property infringement claims under Section 14 of the MSA; (ii) liability arising from a party\'s breach of the confidentiality obligations set forth in Section 6 of the MSA (which liability is subject to a separate super-cap equal to two times (2x) the total annual fees payable under the MSA); (iii) liability arising from a party\'s fraud, gross negligence, or willful misconduct; and (iv) a party\'s obligations to pay fees and expenses properly due and owing under the MSA.

**DPA Liability --- Separate Treatment:** The MSA expressly provides that liability arising from data protection obligations shall be governed exclusively by the terms of the Data Processing Agreement, to be executed as Exhibit D to the MSA (see Section 9 below). The MSA general liability cap does not apply to, and does not subsume, any DPA-specific liability provisions. *Note: The DPA template provided by Stratosphere (Version 3.2, dated January 10, 2025) proposes a separate aggregate data protection liability cap of €500,000 (approximately \$545,000 at current exchange rates). This DPA-specific cap is substantially below the MSA general liability cap and is subject to ongoing negotiation between the parties.*

**Consequential Damages Exclusion:** The MSA contains a mutual exclusion of liability for indirect, incidental, consequential, special, exemplary, and punitive damages, including without limitation lost profits, lost revenue, and loss of business opportunity. This mutual exclusion is subject to carve-outs for: (i) breaches of confidentiality obligations under Section 6 of the MSA; (ii) third-party intellectual property indemnification obligations under Section 14 of the MSA; and (iii) liability arising from fraud, gross negligence, or willful misconduct.
**[Section 6 --- Confidentiality]{.underline}**

The MSA imposes mutual confidentiality obligations on both parties with respect to all Confidential Information (as defined in Section 6.1 of the MSA) disclosed by either party to the other in connection with the MSA. The confidentiality obligations survive for a period of three (3) years following the expiration or termination of the MSA. Standard carve-outs apply for information that is or becomes publicly available without breach by the receiving party, is independently developed by the receiving party without reference to Confidential Information, is lawfully obtained from a third party without restriction, or is required to be disclosed by applicable law, regulation, or valid legal process. The confidentiality provisions of the MSA do not limit, replace, or otherwise affect either party\'s data protection obligations under the Data Processing Agreement.
**[Section 7 --- Insurance]{.underline}**

Stratosphere shall procure and maintain, at its own cost and expense, throughout the term of the MSA and for a period of twenty-four (24) months following its expiration or termination, the following minimum insurance coverage:
> \(a\) Commercial general liability insurance with a minimum coverage of €5,000,000 per occurrence and in the aggregate;
> \(b\) Professional liability / errors and omissions insurance with a minimum coverage of €10,000,000 per occurrence and in the aggregate; and

> \(c\) Cyber liability insurance with a minimum coverage of €5,000,000 per occurrence and in the aggregate, covering data breach response costs, regulatory fines and penalties (to the extent insurable), and network security liability.

Stratosphere shall provide certificates of insurance to Pinnacle upon request and shall notify Pinnacle promptly in writing of any material change to, cancellation of, or failure to renew any required insurance coverage.
**[Section 8 --- Governing Law and Dispute Resolution]{.underline}**

**Governing Law:** The MSA is governed by and shall be construed in accordance with the laws of the State of New York, United States of America, without regard to its conflict of laws principles or provisions that would require or permit the application of the laws of any other jurisdiction.

**Dispute Resolution:** Any dispute, controversy, or claim arising out of or relating to the MSA, including its formation, interpretation, performance, breach, or termination, shall be finally resolved by binding arbitration administered by the American Arbitration Association (\"AAA\") under its Commercial Arbitration Rules then in effect. The seat (legal place) of arbitration shall be New York, New York. The arbitral tribunal shall consist of three (3) arbitrators appointed in accordance with the AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules. The language of the arbitration shall be English. The award rendered by the arbitral tribunal shall be final and binding on the parties, and judgment upon the award may be entered in any court of competent jurisdiction.

**Carve-out for Injunctive Relief:** Notwithstanding the foregoing, nothing in the MSA shall prevent either party from seeking provisional, interim, or injunctive relief from any court of competent jurisdiction at any time, including without limitation relief to prevent unauthorized disclosure of Confidential Information, to enforce intellectual property rights, or to preserve the status quo pending the outcome of arbitration.

**DPA Governing Law --- Separate Treatment:** The MSA acknowledges that the Data Processing Agreement may contain its own governing law and dispute resolution provisions, which shall govern data-protection-specific disputes to the extent expressly provided therein. *Note: The DPA template circulated by Stratosphere (Version 3.2, dated January 10, 2025) specifies the laws of the Federal Republic of Germany as the governing law for all DPA-related matters and provides for arbitration administered by the DIS (Deutsche Institution für Schiedsgerichtsbarkeit e.V. / German Institution of Arbitration) with the seat of arbitration in Munich, Germany, for all DPA-related disputes, including disputes involving the processing of US-origin data. This creates a potential three-way governing law framework: MSA disputes (New York law / AAA, New York); DPA disputes as currently proposed by Stratosphere (German law / DIS, Munich); and Pinnacle\'s internal legal playbook preference for US-specific data processing disputes (Delaware law / US District Court, Western District of Texas, Austin Division). This complexity is noted for purposes of the ongoing DPA negotiation.*
**[Section 9 --- Data Processing Agreement]{.underline}**

**DPA Requirement:** The MSA contemplates that a Data Processing Agreement (\"DPA\") shall be negotiated, finalized, and executed as Exhibit D to the MSA prior to the commencement of any processing of personal data by Stratosphere (or any of its authorized subprocessors) on behalf of Pinnacle or Pinnacle EU under the MSA.

**DPA as Condition Precedent to EU Launch:** The execution of a fully conforming DPA is a condition precedent to the commencement of EU Services under the MSA. The targeted EU Go-Live Date is September 1, 2025.

**Current Status of DPA Negotiation:** Stratosphere circulated its standard DPA template (Version 3.2, dated January 10, 2025) to Pinnacle on April 14, 2025. Pinnacle\'s internal review of the DPA template is targeted for completion by May 16, 2025. The DPA is currently under active review by Pinnacle\'s Office of General Counsel and by Pinnacle\'s outside counsel, Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP, with offices at 900 K Street NW, Suite 700, Washington, DC 20001 (lead partner for this engagement: Rachel Osterfeld).

**Scope of the DPA:** The DPA will cover all processing of personal data by Stratosphere and its authorized subprocessors --- specifically, Larkfield Data Systems, LLC and Orionis Analytics Ltd. --- on behalf of Pinnacle under the MSA, encompassing both US and EU data processing activities across all data center locations and all support access points (including remote access by Singapore-based support engineers).

**Regulatory Framework:** The DPA must address and ensure compliance with the EU General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) (\"GDPR\"), the US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, as amended (\"HIPAA\"), the California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (\"CCPA/CPRA\"), and any other data protection, privacy, or information security laws applicable to the processing activities contemplated under the MSA.
**Stratosphere\'s Outside Counsel for DPA Negotiation:** Voss Kellner Rechtsanwälte, Maximilianstraße 35, 80539 Munich, Germany (lead partner: Dr. Karin Beckert).
**Stratosphere Data Protection Officer:** Dr. Annika Vogt, Data Protection Officer, Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH (contact: dpo@stratospherecloud.example.com).
**[Section 10 --- Certifications and Compliance]{.underline}**
Stratosphere currently holds the following certifications relevant to the services provided under the MSA:

> \(a\) **ISO/IEC 27001:2022** --- Information Security Management Systems. Certificate No. ISO-27001-SC-2024-0891, issued by TÜV Rheinland AG on June 15, 2024, valid through June 14, 2027. The certification covers Stratosphere\'s cloud hosting and managed database services operations at its Frankfurt, Germany and Dublin, Ireland data centers.

> \(b\) **SOC 2 Type II** --- Service Organization Controls Report. Report dated September 30, 2024, covering the audit period from October 1, 2023 through September 30, 2024, issued by Clearwater Audit Partners GmbH (Munich). The report covers the Trust Services Criteria of Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, and Confidentiality.

Stratosphere shall maintain its ISO/IEC 27001 certification in good standing and shall provide updated SOC 2 Type II reports to Pinnacle on an annual basis throughout the term of the MSA. Any material changes to the scope of Stratosphere\'s certifications or any failure to maintain or renew such certifications shall be promptly communicated to Pinnacle in writing.
**[Section 11 --- Termination]{.underline}**

**Termination for Material Breach:** Either party may terminate the MSA upon written notice to the other party if the other party commits a material breach of the MSA and fails to cure such breach within thirty (30) days after receipt of written notice specifying the nature of the breach in reasonable detail.

**Termination for Insolvency:** Either party may terminate the MSA immediately upon written notice if the other party becomes insolvent, makes an assignment for the benefit of creditors, files or has filed against it a petition in bankruptcy or similar proceeding, or has a receiver or trustee appointed for a substantial portion of its assets.

**Termination for Convenience by Client:** The Client may terminate the MSA for convenience upon ninety (90) days\' prior written notice to Stratosphere, subject to payment of all fees for services rendered through the effective date of termination and payment of fees for the remainder of the then-current quarterly invoicing period.

**Post-Termination Obligations:** Upon expiration or termination of the MSA for any reason, the parties\' post-termination obligations shall include transition assistance, data return, and data deletion, in each case as further specified in the DPA and the applicable Statements of Work.
**[Section 12 --- Miscellaneous]{.underline}**

**Entire Agreement:** The MSA, together with all exhibits thereto (including the DPA once executed as Exhibit D), all Statements of Work, and all written amendments and modifications, constitutes the entire agreement between the parties with respect to the subject matter hereof and supersedes all prior and contemporaneous negotiations, understandings, representations, and agreements, whether written or oral.

**Amendment:** The MSA may be amended, modified, or supplemented only by a written instrument duly executed by authorized representatives of both parties. No waiver of any provision of the MSA shall be effective unless made in writing and signed by the party granting such waiver.

**Notices:** All notices, demands, and other communications required or permitted under the MSA shall be in writing and shall be deemed duly given when delivered personally, sent by nationally recognized overnight courier, or sent by registered or certified mail (return receipt requested), addressed as follows:
> If to **Pinnacle:** Margaret Yuen-Park, General Counsel Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc. 4200 Harborview Boulevard, Suite 1100 Austin, TX 78746
> If to **Stratosphere:** Dr. Florian Neumann, Chief Legal Officer Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH Hohenzollernstraße 88 80796 Munich, Germany

**Assignment:** Neither party may assign or transfer its rights or obligations under the MSA without the prior written consent of the other party, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed; provided, however, that either party may assign the MSA without the other party\'s consent in connection with a merger, consolidation, reorganization, or sale of all or substantially all of the assigning party\'s assets, so long as the assignee agrees in writing to be bound by the terms of the MSA.

**Counterparts and Electronic Signatures:** The MSA may be executed in one or more counterparts, each of which shall be deemed an original and all of which together shall constitute one and the same instrument. The parties agree that electronic signatures shall have the same legal force and effect as original ink signatures.

35: **[Section 1: Purpose and Scope of This Playbook]{.underline}**
36: 
37: This playbook sets forth Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc.\'s (\"**Pinnacle**\" or the \"**Company**\") mandatory, preferred, and fallback negotiation positions for Data Processing Agreements (\"**DPAs**\") with third-party vendors and service providers that process personal data on Pinnacle\'s behalf. The purpose of this document is to ensure consistency, regulatory compliance, and efficient negotiation across all vendor DPA engagements by providing Pinnacle\'s legal team and authorized negotiators with clear, tiered guidance on acceptable contractual terms.
38: 
39: Pinnacle is a Delaware corporation operating as a US-based digital health platform company. The Company provides cloud-based electronic health records management, telehealth facilitation, patient engagement tools, and healthcare analytics services to healthcare providers across the United States.
40: 
41: Pinnacle acts as a **HIPAA Covered Entity** for certain data flows involving Protected Health Information (\"**PHI**\") of approximately **2.1 million US patients** and approximately **14,000 US healthcare provider contacts**. These data flows are central to Pinnacle\'s core service offerings and are implicated in the majority of vendor engagements involving clinical and patient-facing data processing activities.
42: 
43: Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents**, triggering obligations under the California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (\"**CCPA/CPRA**\"). Given the significant volume of California resident data processed by Pinnacle and its vendors, CCPA/CPRA compliance is a primary concern in all vendor DPA negotiations involving consumer-facing data.
44: 
45: Pinnacle is expanding into the European Union with a target launch date of **September 1, 2025**. The Company\'s EU operations will be conducted through its wholly owned subsidiary, **Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.**, registered in the Netherlands at Herengracht 450, 1017 CA Amsterdam. Pinnacle EU B.V. will act as Controller under the General Data Protection Regulation (\"**GDPR**\") for an estimated **150,000 projected EU patients** and approximately **320 EU healthcare provider contacts** in Year 1. This EU expansion introduces GDPR obligations that intersect with and complement Pinnacle\'s existing US data protection requirements.
46: 
47: This playbook addresses the following regulatory regimes and their implications for vendor DPA negotiations:
48: 
49: > • **HIPAA/HITECH**, including Business Associate Agreement (\"BAA\") requirements;
50: >
51: > • **CCPA/CPRA**, including Service Provider qualification and certification requirements;
52: >
53: > • **GDPR**, including Article 28 processor requirements and cross-border data transfer mechanisms; and
54: >
55: > • **Pinnacle\'s internal data governance standards**, which in certain areas exceed the minimum requirements of applicable law.
56: 
57: **Important Note:** This playbook does NOT replace the requirement for outside counsel review of DPAs involving novel or high-risk processing activities. Negotiators must escalate to **Rachel Osterfeld** at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP for matters involving cross-border transfers to jurisdictions without adequacy decisions, novel HIPAA scenarios (including first-of-kind technology deployments involving PHI), regulatory enforcement actions or investigations, or any matter where the vendor\'s proposed terms deviate materially from the positions set forth herein and the applicable fallback position is inadequate to protect Pinnacle\'s interests.
58: 
59: **[Section 2: Regulatory Framework Overview]{.underline}**
60: 
61: Pinnacle\'s vendor DPA negotiations must account for three primary regulatory regimes, each of which imposes distinct and, in some cases, overlapping requirements on the contractual relationship between Pinnacle and its data processing vendors. Understanding the interplay among these regimes is essential for effective negotiation. This Section provides a summary overview; detailed negotiation positions for each regime are set forth in the Sections that follow.
62: 
63: The three regimes are: (1) the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, as amended by the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act of 2009 (\"**HIPAA/HITECH**\"); (2) the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020 (\"**CCPA/CPRA**\"); and (3) the General Data Protection Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (\"**GDPR**\"). Each regime imposes its own definitions, obligations, and enforcement mechanisms, and each requires specific contractual provisions in vendor agreements. Where a vendor processes data subject to multiple regimes (which is increasingly common in Pinnacle\'s vendor portfolio), the DPA must address all applicable requirements, and the most restrictive standard generally governs.
64: 
65: Negotiators should be aware that many vendor-provided DPA templates are drafted primarily with GDPR in mind and may fail to address HIPAA or CCPA/CPRA requirements. It is the negotiator\'s responsibility to identify these gaps and require the addition of all necessary provisions before execution.
66: 
67: **[2.1 HIPAA / HITECH]{.underline}**
68: 
69: Pinnacle is a **Covered Entity** under HIPAA as defined in 45 CFR § 160.103. Any vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits Protected Health Information (\"**PHI**\") on Pinnacle\'s behalf qualifies as a **Business Associate** under 45 CFR § 160.103 and is subject to the full range of HIPAA and HITECH requirements applicable to Business Associates.
70: 
71: All DPAs with Business Associates **MUST** incorporate a **Business Associate Agreement** (\"**BAA**\"), either as an integrated section within the DPA body or as a standalone exhibit appended to and expressly incorporated by reference into the DPA. This requirement is non-negotiable and derives from the mandatory contractual provisions set forth in **45 CFR § 164.502(e)** and **45 CFR § 164.504(e)**.
72: 
73: A compliant BAA must include, at a minimum, the following elements:
74: 
75: 1\. **Definitions** of PHI, Covered Entity, and Business Associate consistent with HIPAA regulatory definitions;
76: 
77: 2\. **Permitted uses and disclosures** of PHI, limited to those necessary to perform services under the DPA and Master Services Agreement (\"MSA\"), and consistent with the minimum necessary standard;
78: 
79: 3\. **Minimum necessary standard** compliance (45 CFR § 164.502(b)), requiring the vendor to limit its use, disclosure, and requests for PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of the processing;
80: 
81: 4\. **Workforce training requirements**, obligating the vendor to train all workforce members with access to PHI on HIPAA privacy and security requirements;
82: 
83: 5\. **Breach notification obligations**, requiring prompt notification to Pinnacle, and supporting Pinnacle\'s obligations to notify affected individuals and the Department of Health and Human Services (\"**HHS**\") in accordance with the HITECH Act breach notification provisions;
84: 
85: 6\. **HIPAA Security Rule safeguard categories**, requiring the vendor to implement and maintain reasonable and appropriate administrative safeguards (45 CFR § 164.308), physical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.310), and technical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.312);
86: 
87: 7\. **Subcontractor flow-down of BAA terms**, requiring the vendor to ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on vendor\'s behalf agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to the vendor under the BAA (45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii));
88: 
89: 8\. **Record retention of six (6) years** per 45 CFR § 164.530(j), covering all HIPAA-required documentation including the BAA itself, policies and procedures, training records, and incident records; and
90: 
91: 9\. **Return or destruction of PHI at termination**, with exceptions where return or destruction is infeasible, in which case the protections of the BAA must extend to all retained PHI for as long as it is maintained.
92: 
93: Negotiators should be particularly alert to vendor DPA templates that reference GDPR Article 28 processor requirements but omit any reference to HIPAA. Where a vendor will process PHI, the absence of a BAA renders the DPA non-compliant regardless of how robust the GDPR provisions may be.
94: 
95: **[2.2 CCPA / CPRA]{.underline}**
96: 
97: Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents** across its patient-facing platform, provider network, and marketing and analytics activities. This volume substantially exceeds the CCPA/CPRA applicability thresholds and places Pinnacle squarely within the statute\'s scope as a \"**Business**\" under Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(d).
98: 
99: Vendors that process California personal information on Pinnacle\'s behalf must qualify as \"**Service Providers**\" under Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ag). The Service Provider designation is not automatic; it requires specific contractual provisions that restrict the vendor\'s use, retention, and disclosure of personal information received from Pinnacle. Without these contractual provisions, a vendor may be deemed a \"third party\" under the CCPA/CPRA, which could expose Pinnacle to claims that it has \"sold\" or \"shared\" personal information in violation of the statute.
100: 
101: DPAs with vendors processing California personal information must include the following provisions, which are treated as **must-have** requirements in all negotiations:
102: 
103: > • A **contractual prohibition** on selling or sharing personal information, as those terms are defined in Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ad) (\"sale\") and § 1798.140(ah) (\"share\");
104: >
105: > • A **prohibition on combining** personal information received from Pinnacle with personal information received from any other person or entity, or collected from the consumer\'s own direct interaction with the vendor, except as expressly permitted by the CCPA/CPRA;
106: >
107: > • A **prohibition on using** personal information for any purpose other than the specific business purpose set forth in the DPA or MSA, including any commercial purpose other than providing the services specified in the agreement;
108: >
109: > • A **certification** in which the vendor expressly certifies that it understands these restrictions and will comply with them, as required under CPRA amendments to Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d).
110: 
111: These provisions are mandatory for all vendors with access to California resident data. A vendor DPA that omits these provisions, or that contains language inconsistent with the Service Provider classification, must be redlined before execution. Detailed negotiation positions for CCPA/CPRA terms are set forth in Section 7 of this playbook.
112: 
113: **[2.3 GDPR]{.underline}**
114: 
115: Upon Pinnacle\'s EU expansion, which is scheduled for **September 1, 2025**, Pinnacle (acting through its subsidiary **Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.**) will function as **Controller** under the GDPR for the processing of personal data of EU/EEA data subjects. Vendor DPAs must comply with **GDPR Article 28** processor requirements, which mandate a written contract between the controller and processor that sets forth the subject-matter and duration of processing, the nature and purpose of processing, the types of personal data and categories of data subjects, and the obligations and rights of the controller.
116: 
117: Where personal data is transferred outside the European Economic Area (\"**EEA**\"), appropriate transfer mechanisms must be in place. Acceptable mechanisms include:
118: 
119: > • **EU Standard Contractual Clauses (\"SCCs\")** per Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914, with the appropriate module selected for each transfer relationship;
120: >
121: > • **EU-US Data Privacy Framework** certification, where the receiving entity is certified and the certification covers the relevant data processing activities; and
122: >
123: > • **Binding Corporate Rules**, where applicable and approved by the competent supervisory authority.
124: 
125: GDPR requirements are addressed in this playbook where they intersect with US negotiation positions, particularly with respect to cross-border data transfers, breach notification, data subject rights, and subprocessor obligations. A separate **EU DPA Addendum Checklist** is maintained by outside counsel at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP and should be consulted for all DPAs involving EU data processing. Negotiators working on DPAs with a GDPR component should coordinate with outside counsel to ensure that the EU-specific requirements are fully addressed.
126: 
127: **[Section 3: Definitions --- Required Contractual Definitions]{.underline}**
128: 
129: Every Pinnacle DPA must include clearly defined terms organized by regulatory regime. The inclusion of complete and accurate definitions is essential to ensuring that the DPA\'s operative provisions are enforceable and that each party\'s obligations are unambiguous. This Section sets forth the required defined terms and Pinnacle\'s negotiation positions regarding their inclusion.
130: 
131: **[3.1 Required Defined Terms by Regulatory Regime]{.underline}**
132: 
133: **GDPR Definitions (per Article 4)**
134: 
135: The following terms must be defined consistently with GDPR Article 4:
136: 
137: > • **Personal Data** (Art. 4(1))
138: >
139: > • **Processing** (Art. 4(2))
140: >
141: > • **Controller** (Art. 4(7))
142: >
143: > • **Processor** (Art. 4(8))
144: >
145: > • **Data Subject** (Art. 4(1))
146: >

187: **[3.2 Negotiation Positions for Definitions]{.underline}**

189: **Must-have:** The DPA must include all three sets of definitions where the vendor processes data subject to multiple regulatory regimes. A DPA that covers PHI but lacks the defined term \"Protected Health Information\" creates ambiguity regarding the scope of the vendor\'s obligations and may be insufficient to satisfy the BAA requirements of 45 CFR § 164.504(e). Similarly, a DPA that covers California personal information but lacks the defined terms \"Service Provider,\" \"Sale,\" and \"Share\" may fail to establish the vendor\'s qualification as a Service Provider under the CCPA/CPRA, with potentially significant regulatory consequences for Pinnacle.

The negotiator should confirm that the cross-references are accurate and that the defined terms in the exhibit or addendum are consistent with the terms used in the DPA body.

195: **[Section 4: HIPAA Business Associate Agreement Requirements]{.underline}**
196: 
197: This Section addresses the most critical requirement for US healthcare vendor DPAs: the **HIPAA Business Associate Agreement**. The BAA is not a discretionary contract term; it is a **regulatory mandate** under 45 CFR § 164.502(e) and 45 CFR § 164.504(e). Failure to execute a compliant BAA with a vendor that processes PHI exposes Pinnacle to enforcement action by the HHS Office for Civil Rights (\"**OCR**\"), including civil monetary penalties of up to \$2,067,813 per violation category per calendar year (as adjusted for inflation). Equally important, the absence of a BAA means that any disclosure of PHI to the vendor may itself constitute a HIPAA violation.
198: 
199: ALL vendors that create, receive, maintain, or transmit PHI on Pinnacle\'s behalf must execute a BAA. There are no exceptions to this requirement. This Section sets forth the must-have, nice-to-have, and fallback positions for BAA terms, as well as non-negotiable red lines.
200: 
201: **[4.1 BAA as Must-Have]{.underline}**
202: 
203: **Must-have:** The vendor DPA must include a fully compliant HIPAA BAA, either integrated into the DPA body or attached as a standalone exhibit that is expressly incorporated by reference into the DPA. No DPA may be executed without a BAA where the vendor processes PHI.
204: 
205: The BAA must specify, at a minimum, the following terms:
206: 
207: > **(a) Permitted Uses and Disclosures.** Vendor\'s uses and disclosures of PHI must be limited to those necessary to perform the services described in the DPA and the applicable MSA, and must be consistent with Pinnacle\'s minimum necessary policies. The BAA should enumerate the specific permitted purposes and should include a catch-all restriction providing that any use or disclosure not expressly authorized is prohibited.
208: >
209: > **(b) Minimum Necessary Standard.** The BAA must require vendor compliance with the \"minimum necessary\" standard set forth in 45 CFR § 164.502(b). Vendor must limit its use, disclosure, and requests for PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of each use, disclosure, or request. Vendor must implement policies and procedures to identify the workforce members who need access to PHI and to limit each such workforce member\'s access to the minimum PHI necessary for that person\'s role.
210: >
211: > **(c) Workforce Training.** Vendor must train all workforce members who have access to PHI on HIPAA privacy and security requirements. Training must be provided upon hiring and at least annually thereafter. Vendor must maintain documentation of training completion and make such documentation available to Pinnacle upon reasonable request.
212: >
213: > **(d) HIPAA Security Rule Safeguards.** Vendor must implement and maintain safeguards consistent with the three categories of the HIPAA Security Rule:
214: >
215: > \(i\) **Administrative safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.308, including risk analysis and risk management, security management processes, workforce security, information access management, security awareness and training, security incident procedures, contingency planning, and evaluation;
216: >
217: > \(ii\) **Physical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.310, including facility access controls, workstation use and security, and device and media controls; and
218: >
219: > \(iii\) **Technical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.312, including access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, person or entity authentication, and transmission security.
220: >
221: > **(e) Subcontractor Flow-Down.** Vendor must ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of vendor agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to vendor under the BAA, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii). This flow-down obligation must be contractually documented between vendor and each such subcontractor before PHI is made available to the subcontractor.
222: >
223: > **(f) Breach Notification.** The BAA must include breach notification obligations consistent with the HITECH Act requirements, as described in detail in Section 5 of this playbook.
224: >
225: > **(g) Record Retention.** Vendor must retain HIPAA-required documentation for a period of six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when the document was last in effect, whichever is later, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.530(j). This includes the BAA itself, policies and procedures relating to the protection of PHI, workforce training records, incident response records, and risk assessment documentation.
226: >
227: > **(h) Return or Destruction of PHI at Termination.** Upon termination or expiration of the DPA/MSA, vendor must return or destroy all PHI in its possession, including all copies in any form or medium. Where return or destruction is infeasible (e.g., because PHI is embedded in archived backup systems), vendor must extend the protections of the BAA to all retained PHI and limit further uses and disclosures to those purposes that make return or destruction infeasible. Vendor must certify in writing that it has returned or destroyed all PHI, or that return or destruction is infeasible and identifying the specific PHI retained.
228: 
229: **Nice-to-have:** The BAA should be integrated directly into the DPA body rather than attached as a separate exhibit. Integration reduces the risk of gaps in coverage that can arise when the DPA and BAA are separate documents with potentially inconsistent terms, different effective dates, or different amendment procedures. An integrated BAA also simplifies contract management and ensures that the BAA\'s security and audit provisions are consistent with the corresponding DPA provisions.
230: 
231: **Fallback:** A standalone BAA exhibit is acceptable if the following conditions are met: (i) the BAA exhibit is expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference; (ii) the BAA cross-references the DPA\'s security, audit, and breach notification provisions to ensure consistency; (iii) the BAA is executed simultaneously with the DPA and by the same authorized signatories; and (iv) the BAA includes a provision stating that, in the event of a conflict between the BAA and the DPA, the more protective provision governs with respect to the handling of PHI.
232: 
233: **[4.2 BAA Negotiation Red Lines]{.underline}**
234: 
235: Pinnacle will **NOT** execute a DPA without a conforming BAA where the vendor processes PHI. This is a **non-negotiable requirement** driven by federal law. No business justification, no vendor relationship importance, and no time pressure overrides this requirement.
236: 
237: If a vendor refuses to execute a BAA, or if a vendor\'s proposed BAA is materially deficient and the vendor refuses to negotiate acceptable terms, the negotiator must **escalate immediately** to Margaret Yuen-Park, General Counsel, and to Rachel Osterfeld at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP. Under no circumstances should a negotiator proceed with DPA execution in the absence of a conforming BAA.
238: 
239: For context, Pinnacle currently has approximately **2.1 million US patients** and approximately **14,000 US healthcare provider contacts** whose PHI may be processed by vendors in the course of providing services to Pinnacle. The regulatory and reputational exposure associated with unauthorized disclosure of this PHI is substantial. OCR enforcement actions in recent years have resulted in settlements and penalties ranging from \$100,000 to over \$16 million for HIPAA violations involving inadequate BAA protections.
240: 
241: Negotiators should also be aware that some vendors may propose a \"HIPAA addendum\" or \"healthcare data supplement\" that purports to address HIPAA requirements but does not contain all of the mandatory BAA provisions listed in Section 4.1 above. Such documents must be carefully reviewed against the checklist in Section 4.1, and any missing provisions must be added before execution.

243: **[Section 5: Breach Notification]{.underline}**
244: 
245: Breach notification provisions are among the most operationally significant terms in any DPA. The speed and completeness of vendor breach notification directly affects Pinnacle\'s ability to assess the breach, mitigate harm to affected individuals, and meet its own notification obligations under HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s breach notification requirements, which are in certain respects **more restrictive** than the standalone requirements of any single applicable regulation.
246: 
247: Pinnacle\'s internal data breach response standard, as adopted by the Board of Directors in October 2023, requires that the Company\'s Incident Response Team be activated within **four (4) hours** of receiving vendor notification of a breach or suspected breach. This internal standard drives the 24-hour vendor notification requirement described below; a vendor notification timeline of 48 hours or longer is insufficient to support Pinnacle\'s internal response protocols and downstream regulatory obligations.
248: 
249: **[5.1 Notification Timeline]{.underline}**
250: 
251: **Must-have:** Vendor must notify Pinnacle of any actual or reasonably suspected breach of Personal Data, PHI, or California Personal Information within **twenty-four (24) hours** of discovery. For purposes of this requirement, \"**discovery**\" means the first day on which the breach is known to the vendor, or the first day on which the breach, by exercising reasonable diligence, would have been known to the vendor. This definition is consistent with the HITECH Act\'s definition of discovery at 42 U.S.C. § 17382.
252: 
253: The 24-hour notification obligation applies regardless of whether the breach is confirmed or still under investigation. Pinnacle recognizes that a vendor\'s initial notification may be preliminary and that additional information will become available as the investigation proceeds. However, the failure to provide timely preliminary notification --- even where the full scope of the breach is not yet known --- deprives Pinnacle of the ability to initiate its own assessment and response activities.
254: 
255: Notification must be directed to Pinnacle\'s Chief Privacy Officer, Dr. Anand Krishnamurthy, at privacy-incidents@pinnaclehealth.com and by telephone at (512) 555-0199 (available 24/7), with a copy to the General Counsel\'s office at legal-notices@pinnaclehealth.com.
256: 
257: **Nice-to-have:** Vendor provides **preliminary telephonic notification** within **four (4) hours** of discovery, followed by **written notification** within **twenty-four (24) hours** of discovery. The telephonic notification should include the vendor\'s initial assessment of the nature of the incident, the categories of data potentially affected, and the vendor\'s immediate containment measures. This telephonic-plus-written approach allows Pinnacle\'s Incident Response Team to begin its assessment in parallel with the vendor\'s investigation.
258: 
259: **Fallback:** The 24-hour notification timeline is a **firm requirement**. Pinnacle will not accept timelines exceeding 24 hours for processor-to-controller notification. Negotiators should be aware that many vendor DPA templates propose **48-hour** or **72-hour** notification timelines. These proposals must be rejected and redlined to 24 hours. The following talking points may be useful in negotiations:
260: 
261: > • The **72-hour timeline** referenced in GDPR Article 33(1) is the *controller\'s* obligation to notify the *supervisory authority*, not the processor\'s obligation to notify the controller. GDPR Article 33(2) requires processors to notify controllers \"without undue delay after becoming aware\" of a breach, which the European Data Protection Board has interpreted as requiring notification significantly faster than 72 hours.
262: >
263: > • A **48-hour** processor-to-controller timeline is insufficient because it compresses Pinnacle\'s time to assess the breach, engage legal counsel, activate its incident response plan, and prepare its own regulatory notifications. Under HIPAA, Pinnacle must notify affected individuals within 60 days of discovery, and discovery is deemed to occur when the Business Associate notifies the Covered Entity. Under CCPA/CPRA, California\'s data breach notification statute (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.82) requires notification \"in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.\" Every hour of delay in vendor notification reduces Pinnacle\'s available response window.
264: >
265: > • Pinnacle\'s **24-hour standard** is consistent with market practice for healthcare data processing engagements and is required by multiple state breach notification statutes that apply to Pinnacle.
266: 
267: **[5.2 HIPAA-Specific Breach Notification Obligations]{.underline}**
268: 
269: **Must-have:** The DPA/BAA must include the full HIPAA/HITECH breach notification cascade, reflecting the following obligations:
270: 
271: > **(a)** Vendor (as Business Associate) notifies Pinnacle (as Covered Entity) within **twenty-four (24) hours** of discovery of a breach of Unsecured PHI. This notification triggers Pinnacle\'s own assessment and notification obligations.
272: >
273: > **(b)** Pinnacle notifies affected individuals within **sixty (60) days** of discovery of the breach, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.404. The notification must be in writing, sent by first-class mail to the individual\'s last known address (or by email if the individual has agreed to electronic notice), and must include the elements specified in 45 CFR § 164.404(c).
274: >
275: > **(c)** Pinnacle notifies HHS as follows:
276: >
277: > • For breaches affecting **500 or more individuals**: notification to the HHS Secretary within **sixty (60) days** of discovery, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.408.
278: >
279: > • For breaches affecting **fewer than 500 individuals**: notification to the HHS Secretary no later than **sixty (60) days after the end of the calendar year** in which the breach was discovered, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.408(c).
280: >
281: > **(d)** For breaches affecting **500 or more residents** of a state or jurisdiction, Pinnacle must notify **prominent media outlets** serving that state or jurisdiction within **sixty (60) days** of discovery, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.406.
282: 
283: The DPA/BAA must clearly allocate responsibility for each step of this notification cascade. While vendor (as Business Associate) is responsible for the initial notification to Pinnacle, Pinnacle (as Covered Entity) is responsible for notifications to individuals, HHS, and the media. However, vendor must provide Pinnacle with all information reasonably necessary to enable Pinnacle to fulfill its notification obligations.
284: 
285: **Must-have:** Vendor\'s breach notification to Pinnacle must include, at a minimum, the following information:
286: 
287: > \(i\) The nature of the breach, including a description of what happened and the circumstances of the unauthorized access, use, or disclosure;
288: >
289: > \(ii\) The types of PHI involved in the breach (e.g., names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, diagnoses, treatment information, health plan identification numbers);
290: >
291: > \(iii\) The identification of each individual whose PHI was, or is reasonably believed to have been, accessed, acquired, used, or disclosed as a result of the breach;
292: >
293: > \(iv\) A description of steps that affected individuals should take to protect themselves from potential harm resulting from the breach;
294: >
295: > \(v\) A description of what vendor is doing to investigate the breach, mitigate harm to affected individuals, and prevent future breaches; and
296: >
297: > \(vi\) Contact information for the vendor\'s incident response lead, including name, title, telephone number, and email address.
298: 
299: **Must-have --- Late Notification Penalties:** Breach notification timelines are only meaningful if vendor faces commercial consequences for failure to comply. Pinnacle\'s preferred penalty clause is as follows:
300: 
301: > **Preferred position:** Vendor shall pay Pinnacle liquidated damages of **\$5,000 per day** for each day that vendor\'s breach notification is late (i.e., each day beyond the 24-hour notification deadline), with **no cap** on the total amount of liquidated damages. The parties acknowledge that the harm to Pinnacle from late notification is difficult to quantify and that this amount represents a reasonable estimate of such harm.
302: >
303: > **Fallback:** If the vendor proposes a counter to the liquidated damages provision, Pinnacle will accept a per-day penalty with a reasonable cap, provided that the per-day amount is **no lower than \$2,500** and the cap is **no lower than \$250,000**. Any vendor proposal below these thresholds must be escalated to Margaret Yuen-Park.
304: 
305: **[5.3 Breach Notification Content Requirements]{.underline}**
306: 
307: Regardless of the applicable regulatory regime, all breach notifications from vendor to Pinnacle must include the following minimum content:
308: 
309: > \(a\) The **nature and scope** of the breach, including a description of the incident and the systems, databases, or facilities affected;
310: >
311: > \(b\) The **categories and approximate number of data subjects or individuals** affected by the breach;
312: >
313: > \(c\) The **categories and approximate number of personal data records** affected, including the types of data elements involved;
314: >
315: > \(d\) The **likely consequences** of the breach for affected data subjects or individuals, including an assessment of the risk of identity theft, financial harm, reputational harm, or harm to physical safety;
316: >
317: > \(e\) The **measures taken or proposed** by vendor to address the breach, including containment measures, remediation steps, and measures to prevent recurrence;
318: >
319: > \(f\) The **identity of affected individuals** (where known), to the extent necessary for Pinnacle to fulfill its own notification obligations; and
320: >
321: > \(g\) **Contact information** for the vendor\'s designated incident response lead, including name, title, direct telephone number, and email address, available on a 24/7 basis for the duration of the incident response.
322: 
323: Vendor must provide updates to the initial notification as additional information becomes available, and must cooperate fully with Pinnacle\'s Incident Response Team throughout the investigation and remediation process.

325: **[Section 6: Liability and Indemnification]{.underline}**
326: 
327: Liability provisions are among the most heavily negotiated terms in any DPA. The allocation of financial risk between Pinnacle and its vendors must reflect the magnitude of the data at stake, the severity of potential regulatory penalties, and the operational and reputational harm that a data breach or compliance failure could cause. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s required liability framework, including liability caps, carve-outs, and indemnification obligations.
328: 
329: Pinnacle\'s position on liability is informed by the following considerations: (i) a breach of PHI affecting Pinnacle\'s approximately 2.1 million US patients could result in HIPAA penalties of up to \$2,067,813 per violation category per calendar year, plus class action litigation exposure; (ii) a CCPA/CPRA violation could result in statutory damages of \$100 to \$750 per consumer per incident, which at 890,000 California residents represents potential exposure of \$89 million to \$667.5 million; and (iii) GDPR penalties can reach up to €20 million or 4% of annual worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. Against this backdrop, vendor liability caps that are a fraction of annual fees are commercially unreasonable and legally inadequate.
330: 
331: **[6.1 Liability Cap]{.underline}**
332: 
333: **Must-have:** Vendor\'s aggregate liability for all claims arising under the DPA must be no less than **two times (2x) the total annual fees** attributable to the affected data processing activity.
334: 
335: For reference and illustration:
336: 
337:   ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
338:   **Scenario**                    **Annual Fees**         **Minimum DPA Liability Cap**
339:   ------------------------------- ----------------------- --------------------------------------
340:   Combined US and EU engagement   \$4,200,000             \$8,400,000
341: 
342:   US-only fees                    \$2,800,000             \$5,600,000 (for US-specific claims)
343: 
344:   EU-only fees                    \$1,400,000             \$2,800,000 (for EU-specific claims)
345:   ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
346: 
347: Where fees are allocated by region (e.g., \$2.8 million US and \$1.4 million EU), the cap for EU-specific claims would be no less than \$2,800,000 (2 × \$1,400,000) and for US-specific claims no less than \$5,600,000 (2 × \$2,800,000).
348: 
349: **Must-have:** Liability must be **uncapped** for the following categories of claims:
350: 
351: > \(a\) **Willful misconduct** by vendor, its employees, agents, or subprocessors;
352: >
353: > \(b\) **Gross negligence** by vendor, its employees, agents, or subprocessors;
354: >
355: > \(c\) **Breaches of confidentiality obligations** involving intentional or reckless conduct; and
356: >
357: > \(d\) **Regulatory fines or penalties** imposed on Pinnacle as a direct result of vendor\'s non-compliance with applicable data protection laws, including HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR.
358: 
359: **Must-have:** Consequential, indirect, and special damages may **NOT** be excluded for data breaches involving willful misconduct by vendor. A blanket consequential damages exclusion that applies to all claims, including data protection claims, is unacceptable. While mutual exclusions of consequential damages are common in general commercial agreements, they are inappropriate in the data protection context where the most significant harms to Pinnacle --- including regulatory penalties, class action settlements, breach notification costs, credit monitoring expenses, and reputational damage --- may be characterized as consequential or indirect damages under applicable law. A blanket exclusion could effectively eliminate vendor accountability for the very harms the DPA is intended to address.
360: 
361: **Nice-to-have:** A separate, higher \"**super-cap**\" for data protection claims (e.g., **3x annual fees**) that sits above the general MSA liability cap. This approach allows the parties to maintain a standard liability cap for general commercial claims under the MSA while providing enhanced protection for data protection claims under the DPA. For example, where annual fees are \$4.2 million, the general MSA cap might be \$4.2 million (1x) while the DPA super-cap would be \$12.6 million (3x).
362: 
363: **Fallback:** If vendor insists on a single aggregate cap covering both general commercial claims and data protection claims, the minimum acceptable cap is **2x total annual fees** (\$8,400,000 for a \$4.2 million annual engagement). Pinnacle will not accept a DPA liability cap below this threshold. Any vendor proposal below 2x annual fees must be escalated to Margaret Yuen-Park for review and decision.
364: 
365: **Note for negotiators:** Vendor templates frequently propose caps that are a small fraction of annual fees. It is not uncommon for a vendor with annual fees of several million dollars to propose a DPA liability cap of €500,000 or \$1,000,000. Such caps are commercially unreasonable given the regulatory exposure described above and the volume of data at stake. Negotiators should be prepared to provide the regulatory exposure calculations above as support for Pinnacle\'s 2x annual fees position.
366:

368: 
369: **Must-have:** Vendor must indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Pinnacle, its officers, directors, employees, agents, and affiliates (including Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.) from and against all losses, damages, liabilities, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys\' fees and costs of litigation) arising from or related to:
370: 
371: > \(a\) **Third-party claims** (including claims by data subjects, consumers, patients, and healthcare providers) arising from vendor\'s breach of the DPA, the BAA, or any applicable data protection law;
372: >
373: > \(b\) **Regulatory fines, penalties, assessments, and enforcement costs** imposed on Pinnacle by any governmental authority (including HHS OCR, the California Attorney General, the California Privacy Protection Agency, and any EU/EEA supervisory authority) arising from or related to vendor\'s non-compliance with applicable data protection laws; and
374: >
375: > \(c\) **Costs of breach response**, including but not limited to: costs of breach notification to affected individuals and regulatory authorities; costs of credit monitoring and identity theft protection services provided to affected individuals; costs of forensic investigation; costs of public relations and crisis communications; and costs of regulatory reporting and compliance remediation, in each case to the extent arising from vendor\'s breach of the DPA, the BAA, or applicable data protection law.

377: Indemnification obligations should be subject to the same uncapped/capped structure as direct liability set forth in Section 6.1 above. Specifically, indemnification for claims arising from willful misconduct, gross negligence, intentional breaches of confidentiality, and regulatory fines resulting from vendor non-compliance must be uncapped. Indemnification for all other claims may be subject to the aggregate liability cap (2x annual fees), but must not be subject to any lower cap or sublimit.

381: **[Section 7: CCPA / CPRA Service Provider Requirements]{.underline}**
382: 
383: This Section sets forth the mandatory contractual provisions that must appear in all DPAs where the vendor processes personal information of California residents on Pinnacle\'s behalf. These provisions are required to establish the vendor\'s status as a \"Service Provider\" under the CCPA/CPRA, which is essential to Pinnacle\'s compliance with the statute.
384: 
385: **[7.1 Service Provider Contractual Terms]{.underline}**
386: 
387: **Must-have:** The DPA must include the following CCPA/CPRA Service Provider provisions, consistent with Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d) and § 1798.140(ag):
388: 
389: > **(a) Prohibition on Selling or Sharing.** Vendor is prohibited from selling (as defined in Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ad)) or sharing (as defined in Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ah)) any personal information received from, or on behalf of, Pinnacle. This prohibition applies regardless of whether the vendor receives monetary or other valuable consideration in exchange for the personal information.
390: >
391: > **(b) Purpose Limitation.** Vendor is prohibited from retaining, using, or disclosing personal information received from Pinnacle for any purpose other than performing the services specified in the DPA and the applicable MSA, including any commercial purpose other than providing the services specified in the agreement. Vendor may not use Pinnacle\'s personal information for vendor\'s own business purposes, including but not limited to marketing, product development, analytics, or profiling, unless such use is expressly authorized by Pinnacle in writing and is consistent with a permissible business purpose under the CCPA/CPRA.
392: >
393: > **(c) Restriction to Direct Business Relationship.** Vendor is prohibited from retaining, using, or disclosing personal information received from Pinnacle outside of the direct business relationship between Pinnacle and vendor. This means that vendor may not use Pinnacle\'s personal information to provide services to any other client or customer of vendor, or for any purpose unrelated to the services vendor provides to Pinnacle under the DPA/MSA.
394: >
395: > **(d) Prohibition on Combining.** Vendor is prohibited from combining personal information received from Pinnacle with personal information that vendor receives from or on behalf of any other person or entity, or that vendor collects from the consumer\'s own direct interaction with the vendor, except as expressly permitted by the CCPA/CPRA (e.g., to detect data security incidents or protect against fraud).
396: >
397: > **(e) Service Provider Certification.** Vendor must include a certification, executed by an authorized representative of vendor, stating that vendor understands the restrictions set forth in subparagraphs (a) through (d) above and will comply with them. This certification is a statutory requirement under the CPRA amendments to Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d) and must appear in the DPA itself or in a CCPA/CPRA Addendum appended to the DPA.
398: >
399: > **(f) Right to Monitor Compliance.** Vendor must grant Pinnacle the right to take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure that vendor uses personal information in a manner consistent with Pinnacle\'s obligations under the CCPA/CPRA. This includes the right to conduct ongoing manual reviews, automated scans, and assessments of vendor\'s systems and practices as they relate to the processing of personal information received from Pinnacle.
400: >
401: > **(g) Notification of Inability to Comply.** Vendor must notify Pinnacle promptly if vendor determines that it can no longer meet its obligations under the CCPA/CPRA. Upon receipt of such notification, Pinnacle shall have the right to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate the unauthorized use of personal information, up to and including termination of the DPA/MSA.
